cues.text: Cedric was obviously part of the school when I was a student.
So really my contact with Cedric came about as a student.
He was in the building a lot. He was no longer teaching.
He was involved in a number of high profile projects.
So he redesigned the South Bank for instance and so on.
He did a project for the South Bank and so on.
But he was a character. He was a friend of Alvin's. He came to Jury's.
So basically the wit and intelligence that Cedric had was something that you experienced firsthand.
It wasn't, I mean, it would be wrong to say he didn't play to the gallery.
I think like Peter Cook, he was a character who played to the gallery.
So whenever he spoke, he wanted the room to be listening.
But I think he was also an incredible intelligence.
So he would react to what you said or what was actually put in front of him.
So my first meetings with him were always at juries.
So he was there.
He was pampered and spoilt by Alvin.
So there's famous stories, you know, he'd be given a cigar as he came in
and a bottle of brandy would appear under his chair
and he would sit there and just fill his glass up and talk.
So there were in those days quite a number of high profile juries as it were,
where people came from outside and so on, and you know,
you as one as a student went to all these things to see what was said.
And I think right from first year, I think going to these public juries,
you suddenly realise that Cedric was something that someone who you would go home and ponder about what he said.
And I think what was always really important was that he never said anything in an academic way.
He never said anything like a sort of professor or a teacher.
He would sort of remark on something.
It's rare to meet someone in the architectural environment in particular who is willing to talk about private things.
You know, I think architects are quite facade-like.
you know they wear black and they do this and they behave in a particular way and they only talk
about design um and i i think you know me personally you know i talk about fishing and

warmth and admiration which i think is part of this friendship because you were sharing
and understanding of what was around you,
not simply because you were sort of architects
who were being sort of portrayed.
Yeah, I think the uniqueness
was actually the level of sort of invention
and imagination that he could bring to the conversation,
a level of unpredictability,
a level of easy intelligence.
So in many ways,
when I say that a lot is written
and said and a lot is quoted and you know they're the archive of his tapes and I go to all these

So even the way Cedric looked was extraordinary.
He looked like a politician in a sense, with his hairstyle.
He looked like an old-fashioned Englishman with his thing all pulled back and his cigar.

I mean, it's sort of complete.
He was a mixture between, I suppose, the foot area was like a sort of geography teacher,
the trousers were like school uniform, and the top was like a sort of bowler hat city

I mean, unique even to look at.
In a sense he was, you know, his hair was always come back with sort of hair gel and

Nigel Coates, who then came to teach me how to have his glasses and looked the part.

And Cedric was an anachronism.

because I think a lot of the things I then went on to do
had this Englishness that I'm talking about,
this sort of slight eccentricity.

when I was in diploma school,
when I was in Dip 10 and so on,
it was all kind of old-fashioned shirts

and, you know, it was sort of some weird mixture

There is a key relationship between what I call physical and social structures,
i.e. that space is made up of the relationship between those two things.
So therefore I think the Fun Palace sort of in a sense sums that up.
It suggests the idea that space is never just a space that gets inhabited.
So it's a bit like the comment I was saying about the AA.
The AA didn't exist and Cedric came to it.

I think that in terms of the grittiness of how the projects were presented,
I think that that light-hearted attitude that he had, which I mentioned before,
possibly would be out of place today,

Yes, I think Cedric's emphasis on enabling, I think, is very, very important.
I think, possibly, it's something that he never articulated
beyond the realm of architecture.
and I think it's something that is very close to my heart.
So I think the idea of an architect not simply being a sort of form maker
